io.title: What goes in. What comes out.
io.why: A few sentences are enough. The more facts you give, the fewer blanks are left for you to fill.
io.ins: Who it is for, what a visitor should do, the facts
Photos and a logo, dropped in with your request
A menu, a price list or a CV, read for its facts
A collection in {name}, shown on a page as it is now
io.outs: One to five pages, their links working, as a phone, a tablet or a computer shows them
At an address you pick, for a year from each time you publish
Plain HTML and CSS, to host wherever you like
Gathered into a collection of yours, a row for each
exact.title: Checked before you see it.
exact.why: A site that looks fine on your screen can be cut on a phone, or say nothing to a screen reader. {name} checks every page, tells the AI what to fix, and shows you the site once it is fixed.
exact.cards: On a phone and on a computer, for screen readers and for search engines: nothing cut, links that lead somewhere, colours that read by day and by night, a title and a description for each page.
An address, a price or an opening hour you didn’t give is left as a blank in square brackets, and listed for you to fill in. No invented review, client or award.
Retype any words right on the page, or point at a part and say what to change. What the AI changes afterwards waits for you to accept or reject.
where.title: Where your site lives.
where.why: On your device, until you decide otherwise. Online only when you publish it, and only you can.
where.cards: Your site is plain files in your browser, encrypted. Until you publish it, nothing we can read reaches us.
Sent to the AI you chose
Your request and what you attach go to the AI you picked, and nowhere else. Under every answer, {name} says where it was done.
Online only when you say so
The AI can’t publish: only you do, from a button, each time. Take the site offline whenever you like.
catch.items: {name} is free; the AI behind it may not be. Without a sign-up, only the AI on this computer answers.
Pictures come from your own files, or from an AI that draws when you ask for one, never from the web. Nothing on your site loads from another site.
A site is pages people read and forms that reach you. It has no accounts, no sign-in, no payments and no bookings: for those, it links to the service you already use.
Online, your site is at a name you pick followed by .hst.ing, for a year from each time you publish. For a domain name of your own, download its files and host them where you like.
The host takes files of 10 MB and sites of 50 MB at most, and keeps what visitors send a form, sealed, for a month at most.
{name} can be wrong. Read the site as you would a colleague’s draft before you publish it.
faq.items: Yes, with no account at {name}. The AI that answers may want one: {free} opens a free one, or use a plan you already pay for, or the AI on this computer, with no account at all.
Do I need to know how to code?
No. You say what the site is for, in your own words, and change it the same way. The files are plain HTML and CSS, there if a developer ever wants them.
How do I put it online?
Press {publish} in the site’s pane and pick an address: anyone can then open it, and search engines can find it. You can also download its files and host them anywhere.
Yes. Retype words right on the page, point at a part and say what to change, or ask for anything else in a sentence. Publish again and only what changed is sent.
Yes. Every page is checked at a phone’s width before you see it, and you can look at it as a phone, a tablet or a computer shows it.
Can the site be in several languages?
Yes: ask for them. Each language gets every page, with a switch at the top, and right-to-left languages read the right way round.
